quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Have' plus a past participle links a past action to now, without saying exactly when.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + 'have' + past participle (visited) + object (Japan) + frequency (twice). Present perfect describes experience without naming a specific time.
quests.textToSpeak: I have visited Japan twice.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Never' slides between 'has' and the past participle, just like other adverbs of frequency.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + 'has' + 'never' + past participle (tried) + object (sushi). 'Never' with present perfect means 'not once in her life so far'.
quests.textToSpeak: She has never tried sushi.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Already' emphasizes that something happened sooner than expected.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'have' + 'already' + past participle (finished) + object (the report). 'Already' highlights that a task is complete, often ahead of schedule.
quests.textToSpeak: We have already finished the report.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Since' names the starting point of something that's still true now.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + 'has' + past participle (lived) + place (here) + 'since 2015'. 'Since' marks the exact point when a continuing situation began.
quests.textToSpeak: He has lived here since 2015.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'For' measures a length of time, unlike 'since' which names a starting point.
quests.explanation: Subject (They) + 'have' + past participle (worked) + 'together' + 'for six years'. 'For' pairs with a duration, while 'since' pairs with a starting moment.
quests.textToSpeak: They have worked together for six years.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Yet' at the end of a present perfect question asks if something has happened up to now.
quests.explanation: 'Have' + subject (you) + past participle (finished) + object (your homework) + 'yet'? 'Yet' in questions checks whether an expected action has occurred.
quests.textToSpeak: Have you finished your homework yet?

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The longer background action uses 'was' plus '-ing'; the shorter interruption stays simple past.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (I was cooking, ongoing) + 'when' + clause 2 (the phone rang, sudden). Past continuous sets the scene; past simple interrupts it.
quests.textToSpeak: I was cooking when the phone rang.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: Both actions happened at the same time here — listen for 'while' linking two ongoing moments.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (She was reading) + 'while' + clause 2 (he cleaned the kitchen). 'While' can connect two actions happening simultaneously, not just an interruption.
quests.textToSpeak: She was reading while he cleaned the kitchen.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The ongoing scene comes first, and the sudden arrival breaks into it.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (They were arguing, ongoing) + 'when' + clause 2 (I walked in, sudden). The speaker's arrival interrupts an already-happening situation.
quests.textToSpeak: They were arguing when I walked in.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: This time 'while' opens the sentence, with the continuous clause first.
quests.explanation: 'While' + clause 1 (I was driving, ongoing) + clause 2 (it started to rain, sudden). 'While' can lead the sentence instead of sitting in the middle.
quests.textToSpeak: While I was driving, it started to rain.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The sudden event comes first this time, and 'while' introduces the background action after it.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (He broke his arm, sudden) + 'while' + clause 2 (he was skiing, ongoing). Word order for 'while' clauses can shift without changing the meaning.
quests.textToSpeak: He broke his arm while he was skiing.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Went off' is a fixed phrase meaning 'started ringing suddenly' — it's not literally leaving.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (We were sleeping, ongoing) + 'when' + clause 2 (the alarm went off, sudden). 'Go off' is an idiomatic phrasal verb meaning an alarm starts sounding.
quests.textToSpeak: We were sleeping when the alarm went off.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Came across' means 'found by chance' — the whole phrase carries that one meaning.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + phrasal verb (came across) + object (an old photo) + time (yesterday). 'Come across' means to find something unexpectedly.
quests.textToSpeak: I came across an old photo yesterday.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Put off' means to delay — and 'until spring' shows the new, later timing.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'had to' + phrasal verb (put off) + object (the trip) + 'until spring'. 'Put off' means to postpone something to a later time.
quests.textToSpeak: We had to put off the trip until spring.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Figured out' means 'understood after effort' — 'finally' shows it took some time.
quests.explanation: Subject (My colleague) + adverb (finally) + phrasal verb (figured out) + object (the problem). 'Figure out' means to solve or understand something through thought.
quests.textToSpeak: My colleague finally figured out the problem.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Make an impression' is a fixed pairing — 'do' would sound wrong here.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + frequency (always) + verb (makes) + object (a good impression). English pairs specific verbs with specific nouns, like 'make' with 'impression'.
quests.textToSpeak: He always makes a good impression.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Do a favor' is the correct pairing, unlike 'make a favor' which learners often say by mistake.
quests.explanation: 'Could' + subject (you) + verb (do) + object (me) + object 2 (a quick favor)? 'Do' pairs naturally with 'favor', not 'make'.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you do me a quick favor?

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Take time off' is another fixed collocation, meaning to pause from work.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'need to' + verb (take) + object (some time off). 'Take time off' is a set expression for taking a break from work or duties.
quests.textToSpeak: We need to take some time off.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'I was wondering if' is a soft, indirect way to ask for something, gentler than 'can you'.
quests.explanation: 'I was wondering if' + subject (you) + 'could' + verb (help) + object (me). This past continuous form politely softens a direct request.
quests.textToSpeak: I was wondering if you could help me.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'I suppose' softens the suggestion that follows, making it feel less like a command.
quests.explanation: 'I suppose' + clause (we should leave a bit earlier). 'Suppose' expresses a tentative opinion rather than a firm statement.
quests.textToSpeak: I suppose we should leave a bit earlier.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Seems to be' softens the claim — it's an impression, not a stated fact.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + 'seems to be' + gerund (avoiding) + object (the question). 'Seems to' expresses an impression rather than a certain fact.
quests.textToSpeak: She seems to be avoiding the question.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: An intention meets an obstacle, joined by 'but' right at the pause.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (I wanted to call) + 'but' + clause 2 (the signal was too weak). 'But' introduces an obstacle that blocked the first intention.
quests.textToSpeak: I wanted to call, but the signal was too weak.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'So' connects the free time he had to the kind offer that followed.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (He finished early) + 'so' + clause 2 (he offered to help us). 'So' shows the second action as a natural result of the first.
quests.textToSpeak: He finished early, so he offered to help us.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Although' introduces a downside that doesn't cancel out the positive feeling.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (She likes the job) + 'although' + clause 2 (the commute is long). 'Although' admits a drawback while keeping the main opinion intact.
quests.textToSpeak: She likes the job, although the commute is long.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Since' here means 'because', and it opens the sentence with the reason first.
quests.explanation: 'Since' + reason (it's raining) + result (we should reschedule the picnic). 'Since' at the start of a sentence often means 'because', not 'from that time'.
quests.textToSpeak: Since it's raining, we should reschedule the picnic.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Even though' introduces a fact that would normally stop the action, but didn't.
quests.explanation: 'Even though' + clause 1 (he was tired) + clause 2 (he kept working). 'Even though' shows the second action happened despite the first fact.
quests.textToSpeak: Even though he was tired, he kept working.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: This time 'since' comes in the middle, still meaning 'because'.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (The intern took the bus) + 'since' + clause 2 (her car broke down). 'Since' meaning 'because' can appear at the start or in the middle of a sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: The intern took the bus since her car broke down.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: A present perfect fact leads into 'so' and its natural, present-tense consequence.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (I've already eaten) + 'so' + clause 2 (I'm not very hungry). Present perfect explains a current state through a completed action.
quests.textToSpeak: I've already eaten, so I'm not very hungry.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The ongoing wait sets the scene, and the sudden call breaks into it, just like earlier interrupted-action patterns.
quests.explanation: 'While' + clause 1 (we were waiting, ongoing) + clause 2 (the manager finally called back, sudden). This combines the 'while' pattern from earlier levels with a natural resolution.
quests.textToSpeak: While we were waiting, the manager finally called back.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Three ideas layer together: an ongoing fact, its starting point, and a contrast that doesn't change it.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (She has worked here since she graduated) + 'even though' + clause 2 (the commute is difficult). Present perfect with 'since' can combine with a contrast clause in one longer, natural sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: She has worked here since she graduated, even though the commute is difficult.
